title: Integrating Landsat and ECOSTRESS to explore the value of additional thermal infrared satellite observations for field-scale evapotranspiration mapping
Twin-satellite constraints from GF-5B and DQ-1 enable hourly near-surface NO2 estimation across China
abstract: Nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ) is a major air pollutant with significant impacts on human health, yet satellite-based estimates of surface NO 2 with full diurnal coverage remain limited. Here, we develop a machine learning framework to estimate hourly near-surface NO 2 concentrations across China by integrating complementary observations from two Chinese polar-orbiting satellites, GF-5B (~10:30 local time) and DQ-1 (~13:30 local time). A Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) model driven by twin-satellite NO 2 vertical column densities (VCDs) and meteorological reanalysis achieves strong predictive performance in 10-fold cross-validation, with a coefficient of determination (R 2 ) of 0.91 and root mean square error (RMSE) of 5.40 μg/m 3 across all hours (4.46 μg/m 3 during daytime; 6.32 μg/m 3 at night), and retains reasonable skill under stricter site-based, time-based, and independent cross-year validation. The reconstructed dataset captures the characteristic diurnal cycle of NO 2 , with morning and evening peaks associated with traffic emissions and a midday minimum driven by photochemical loss. Compared to the single-satellite TROPOMI product, the twin-satellite configuration substantially improves the representation of diurnal variability, increasing R 2 from 0.81 to 0.91 and reducing RMSE by 31.60%, and corrects a distorted urban-rural NO 2 exposure ratio (1.70 for TROPOMI versus a ground-based 1.19), narrowing it to 1.30. Feature-importance analysis further shows that meteorological variables dominate model predictions during both day and night, with satellite VCDs providing a complementary, though indirect, constraint on nighttime concentrations. The resulting hourly NO 2 dataset demonstrates the value of synergistic multi-satellite observations for air quality monitoring and provides a robust basis for refined pollution control and population exposure assessment.

title: Advanced characterization of the diurnal variations of aerosol optical and microphysical properties by SYREMIS/GRASP synergistic retrieval algorithm using observations from multiple spaceborne sensors
abstract: Accurate characterization of the diurnal variation of aerosol optical and microphysical properties—including Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD), Angstrom Exponent (AE), and Single Scattering Albedo (SSA)—is fundamental for climate and air quality modeling. However, retrieving high-temporal-resolution, physically consistent aerosol products from multiple satellite instruments remains a challenge. Current multi-satellite approaches often rely on “post-retrieval” merging of independent Level-2 products, a process that frequently introduces physical inconsistencies and artificial temporal oscillations. To address this, building upon the recently established SYREMIS/GRASP synergetic retrieval framework (Litvinov et al., 2025), an inversion approach based on harmonized Level-1 satellite measurements, this study extensively evaluates its performance in capturing aerosol diurnal variability. We evaluate two configurations: (i) LEO + LEO synergy (Sentinel-3 A/B OLCI and Sentinel-5P TROPOMI) and (ii) LEO + GEO synergy (integrating Himawari-8 AHI). By enforcing multi-pixel smoothness constraints within the retrieval, SYREMIS maintains high physical consistency across instruments, effectively mitigating the structural discrepancies and “noise” inherent in standard merging techniques. Our validation against AERONET ground-based data and intercomparison with the XAERDT product suite confirm that SYREMIS provides high retrieval stability and accuracy. Without applying post-retrieval quality filtering, SYREMIS achieves an AOD GCOS fulfillment percentage of up to 70%, an AE RMSE below 0.3, and an SSA “Optimal” requirement fulfillment rate of up to 85% at representative sites. We demonstrate the framework's capability to resolve rapid aerosol dynamics through case studies of biomass-burning events over Thailand and Myanmar, as well as dust pollution over Qatar in 2019. As a three-month proof-of-concept assessment (March–May 2019) , these results highlight the practical capability of the established SYREMIS/GRASP approach to generate high-resolution, physically consistent, and stable aerosol data records from the measurements of multiple satellites.

title: Constructive solid geometry for automatic topology-aware BIM reconstruction from point clouds
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: The automatic reconstruction of Building Information Models (BIMs) remains challenging, especially when applied to multi-storey buildings and indoor environments with non-Manhattan layouts and curved structures. To address these challenges, this paper presents a novel method that places Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) at the core of building reconstruction from point clouds. The methodology also integrates the Segment Anything Model (SAM) and knowledge-based rules to reconstruct as-built BIMs while preserving the geometry and topology of building elements. The proposed approach consists of two main stages: SAM-based segmentation and CSG-based modelling. First, SAM is used to segment rooms, as well as door and window openings. Solids are then generated for the indoor spaces and openings. Finally, a set of Boolean operations is applied to reconstruct building elements, including slabs, walls, indoor spaces, doors, and windows, while subtracting openings of doors, windows, and staircases. Finally, the reconstructed model is encoded with semantic information following the Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) schema. The method was evaluated on seven two-storey building point clouds and demonstrated strong performance, achieving a mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) greater than 90% for floor plan reconstruction, a precision above 87% for door and window detection, and mean geometric deviations below 8 cm for BIM reconstruction.

title: A GeoAI framework for remote-sensing-driven traffic activity and emission intensity in a data-scarce megacity
abstract: ================================================================================FRAMEWORK PIPELINE LOGIC – GeoAI for Traffic Activity & Exposure Mapping================================================================================ This document explains how the six core scripts work together to reconstructtraffic emissions and exposure in Kinshasa, a data‑scarce megacity. The pipeline transforms three primary data sources: - Satellite imagery (Airbus 15 cm) → vehicle counts via YOLOv8 - GTFS transit schedules → bus trajectories, speeds, frequencies - OpenStreetMap + VIIRS night‑time lights → land‑use attraction weights ... into hourly, road‑segment‑level NOx and PM2.5 emission maps. ================================================================================OVERVIEW (STEP‑BY‑STEP)================================================================================ Step 0 – YOLOv8 Vehicle Detection (yolo_kinshasa_powerful.py)────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────- Input: High‑resolution satellite images (train/val split) with YOLO labels (class: bus / priv).- Output: Trained YOLOv8x model + detection counts on validation images.- Purpose: Establish empirical baseline of vehicle counts and compute the bus‑to‑private vehicle ratio. This ratio later calibrates the gravity model. Step 1 – LLM Semantic Classification (llm_classify_landuse.py)────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────- Input: Raw OSM land‑use polygons and points (chaotic metadata).- Output: Shapefiles with a standardised "traffic_class" attribute (Residential, Market_Trade, CBD_Admin, etc.).- Purpose: Assign diurnal activity weights to each land‑use category, enabling the gravity model to attract vehicles to different areas depending on time of day (morning, midday, evening, night). Step 2 – GTFS to Bus Traffic (gtfs_to_bus_traffic.py)────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────- Input: Raw GTFS .txt files (trips, shapes, stop_times, frequencies).- Output: Four interval shapefiles (morn, midday, aftnoon, night) with 1 km segmented bus routes, each containing: - buses_per_hour (frequency) - avg_speed_ms (average speed) - traf_load (vehicle‑hours per hour)- Purpose: Create the deterministic layer of public transit activity. Step 3 – Hub‑and‑Spoke Gravity Model (gravity_model.py)────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────- Inputs: - LLM‑classified land‑use polygons/points (Step 1) - Night‑time lights raster (economic proxy) - Road network shapefile (1 km segmented, snapped) - YOLO‑derived total private vehicle count (from Step 0 ratio)- Output: Roads_24h_Master.shp with hourly private vehicle volumes (V_00h … V_23h) and daily total (Veh_Day).- Purpose: Distribute the city‑wide private fleet across the road network using a potential‑field approach. Attraction weights vary by time block (Morning, Mid‑Day, Evening, Night) based on LLM categories. NTL radiance acts as a wealth/activity proxy. Step 4 – Speed Simulation (speed_simulation.py)────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────- Inputs: - Roads_24h_Master.shp (private volumes) - GTFS bus shapefiles (road_traffic_h{hh}.shp, from Step 2)- Output: speed_analysis_h{hh}.shp for each hour, containing: - Est_Speed (estimated private vehicle speed, km/h) - Traf_Load (volume × travel time) - Uncert (combined uncertainty index)- Purpose: For hours 05–21, spatially join each private road segment to the nearest bus‑observed segment. If found, car speed = min(bus_speed × 1.64, speed_limit). If not found, apply city‑wide congestion index to the speed limit. For night hours (22–04), speed = 0.9 × speed limit. Step 5 – Emission Calculation (emission_calculation.py)────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────- Inputs: - speed_analysis_h{hh}.shp (private speeds & volumes) - road_traffic_h{hh}.shp (bus volumes & speeds)- Output: emiss_priv_h{hh}.shp and emiss_bus_h{hh}.shp with: - EF_NOx, EF_PM25 (speed‑dependent COPERT Tier 3 factors) - E_NOx_g, E_PM25_g (mass emitted per segment, grams) - U_Emiss (propagated uncertainty)- Purpose: Convert traffic activity into chemical mass using: NOx_bus = 372.2/v + 12.8 NOx_priv = 1.54 * v^-0.45 PM2.5_bus = 18.5/v + 0.38 PM2.5_priv = 0.015 (constant, high‑sulfur gasoline) ================================================================================DATA FLOW SUMMARY (WHAT PRODUCES WHAT)================================================================================ Raw OSM → LLM script → LLM‑classified polygons (traffic_class)Raw GTFS → GTFS script → Bus route segments (buses_per_hour, speed)Satellite images → YOLO script → Vehicle counts + bus/priv ratioNTL raster + roads → (direct input to gravity model) LLM polygons + NTL + roads + total private count (from YOLO) → Gravity model → Roads_24h_Master.shp (private V_*h) Roads_24h_Master + bus GTFS shapefiles → Speed simulation → speed_analysis_h*.shp (Est_Speed) speed_analysis + bus GTFS shapefiles → Emission calculation → emiss_priv_h*.shp, emiss_bus_h*.shp ================================================================================KEY ASSUMPTIONS & LIMITATIONS (EMBEDDED IN CODE)================================================================================- Speed multiplier (bus→car): 1.64 (Tétreault & El‑Geneidy, 2010).- Night bus headway = afternoon headway × 0.85 (empirical).- Emission factors: Euro II/III for buses, Euro III/IV for private, with elevated PM2.5 constant for private (0.015 g/km) due to high‑sulfur fuel.- Uncertainty: propagated from YOLO (±15%), speed multiplier variation (±6%), gravity model entropy, and road class risk.- No secondary pollutant formation (ozone, secondary PM) – only primary exhaust. ================================================================================HOW TO VERIFY THE PIPELINE (TEST WITH ONE HOUR)================================================================================1. Run YOLO script → get bus/priv ratio.2. Run LLM script → classify land‑use.3. Run GTFS script → produce bus intervals.4. Run gravity model with total private count = (YOLO priv count) × scaling.5. Run speed simulation for e.g., hour 10.6. Run emission calculation for hour 10.7. Compare emiss_priv_h10 and emiss_bus_h10 outputs with manuscript results. All scripts are designed to run sequentially; each one’s output directoryis hard‑coded as input to the next. Adjust paths in each script to matchyour folder structure. ================================================================================CONTACT================================================================================For questions or to report issues: Ju Wang – wangju@jlu.edu.cn
